claims.text: The onset and progression of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are controlled by preferential surface segregation of Cu.
Cu has a significantly lower melting point than the other constituent elements.
Cu has a lower surface energy than the other constituent elements.
Cu migrates to the nanoparticle surface upon heating because of constituent differences in surface energy and melting point.
Surface segregation produces a thin Cu-rich, liquid-like layer below the bulk melting point.
The Cu-rich surface layer premelts at a lower temperature than the underlying matrix.
The premelted surface layer accelerates inward melting through enhanced atomic mobility, diffusion, and coalescence of adjacent liquid regions.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are initially solid and have a near-homogeneous elemental distribution.
A passivating surface coating can inhibit Cu segregation or surface diffusion.
The controlled comparison is between unmodified and surface-treated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles heated under otherwise identical inert or vacuum conditions.
The experiment is bounded to nanoparticles with similar, controlled sizes of approximately 10–50 nm, defined heating rates, and negligible oxidation or impurity effects.
Unmodified nanoparticles will develop a Cu-rich, liquid-like surface layer earlier than segregation-inhibited nanoparticles.
Unmodified nanoparticles will have a lower detectable premelting-onset temperature than segregation-inhibited nanoparticles.
Unmodified nanoparticles will melt more gradually from the surface inward relative to the uniform-melting baseline.
Without Cu segregation, compositionally uniform nanoparticles would melt more uniformly at a temperature near the bulk melting point of the composite alloy.
In situ TEM can measure the appearance and spatial progression of a liquid-like surface layer.
Elemental mapping can quantify Cu enrichment at the nanoparticle surface.
DSC melting endotherms can be used to compare melting-onset temperatures between coated and uncoated nanoparticles.
The hypothesis is falsified if coated and uncoated particles have the same premelting onset and similar melting progression while showing no significant surface Cu enrichment.
Size-dependent melting-point depression and effects of Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co on local energy landscapes may also contribute to the thermal response.
